source_text: Ἔτι δ᾿ ἐπεὶ βούλεται μηδὲ ἀνεπίληπτον γεγονέναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν ὁ Κέλσος, παραστησάτω. τίς τῶν ἀρεσκομένων τῷ λόγῳ αὐτοῦ τὸ ἀληθῶς ἐπίληπτον τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀνέγραψεν· ἢ, εἰ μὴ ἀπὸ τούτων αὐτοῦ κατηγορεῖ ὡς ἐπιλήπτου, δεικνύτω, πόθεν μαθὼν οὐκ ἀνεπίληπτον αὐτὸν εἴρηκεν. ἐποίησε μὲν οὖν ἃ ἐπηγγείλατο πιστὰ δι᾿ ὧν ὠφέλησε τοὺς προσέχοντας αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς. καὶ ἀεὶ ὁρῶντες πληρούμενα τὰ εἰρημένα ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ, πρὶν γένηται, τὸ „κηρυχθῆναι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον“ ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ, καὶ πορευθέντας αὐτοῦ τοὺς μαθητὰς εἰς „πάντα τὰ ἔθνη“ τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ κατηγγελκέναι, ἔτι δὲ περὶ τοῦ „ἐπὶ ἡγεμόνας καὶ βασιλεῖς“ ἀχθήσεσθαι μέλλειν δι᾿ οὐδεμίαν ἄλλην αἰτίαν ἢ τὴν διδασκαλίαν αὐτοῦ, τεθήπαμεν αὐτὸν καὶ ὁσημέραι βεβαιοῦμεν τὴν εἰς αὐτὸν πίστιν. οὐκ οἶδα δ᾿ ἀπὸ ποίων μειζόνων καὶ ἐναργεστέρων ἐβούλετο αὐτὸν πιστὰ ποιῆσαι τὰ προειρημένα ὁ Κέλσος· εἰ μὴ ἄρα. ὡς φαίνεται. μὴ ἐπιστάμενος τὸν λόγον τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἄνθρωπον γενόμενον ἐβούλετο μηδὲν ἀνθρώπινον παθεῖν μηδὲ γενέσθαι ἀνθρώποις παράδειγμα γενναῖον περὶ τοῦ φέρειν τὰ συμβαίνοντα. κἂν οἴκτιστα τῷ Κέλσῳ ταῦτ᾿ εἶναι δοκῇ καὶ ἐπονειδιστότατα. ἐπεὶ πόνον μὲν τὸ μέγιστον οἶδε τῶν κακῶν ἡδονὴν δὲ τὸ τέλειον ἀγαθὸν, ὅπερ οὐδεὶς τῶν πρόνοιαν εἰσαγόντων φιλοσόφων καὶ ἀνδρίαν ὁμολογούντων εἶναι ἀρετὴν καὶ καρτερίαν καὶ μεγαλοψυχίαν παρεδέξατο· οὐ διέβαλεν οὖν τὴν εἰς αὐτὸν πίστιν ὁ Ἰησοῦς δι᾿ ὧν ὑπέμεινεν, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἐν τοῖς ἀνδρίαν ἀποδέξασθαι βουλομένοις ἐκράτυνε καὶ ἐν τοῖς διδαχθεῖσιν ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ τὸ μὲν κυρίως καὶ ἀληθῶς ζῆν τὸ μακάριον οὐκ εἶναι ἐνταῦθα ἀλλ᾿ „ἐν τῷ“ καλουμένῳ κατὰ τοὺς λόγους αὐτοῦ „μέλλοντι αἰῶνι,“ τὸ δ᾿ ἐν τῷ ἐνεστῶτι αἰῶνι λεγομένῳ ζῆν συμφορὰν εἶναι ἢ ἀγῶνα τὸν πρῶτον καὶ μέγιστον τῆς ψυχῆς.
pass_a_gloss: Further, since Celsus wishes Jesus not even to have been blameless (ἀνεπίληπτος), let him show it (παρίστημι). Who of those pleased with (ἀρέσκομαι) his teaching (λόγος) recorded (ἀναγράφω) the truly blameworthy (ἐπίληπτον) of Jesus? Or, if not from these he accuses (κατηγορέω) him as blameworthy, let him show from where having learned he has said he was not blameless. Jesus therefore did (ποιέω) what he promised (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) credible (πιστά), through the things by which he benefited (ὠφελέω) those attending (προσέχω) to him. And always seeing fulfilled (πληρόω) the things said by him before they happen: that the gospel (εὐαγγέλιον) be preached (κηρύσσω) in the whole world (κόσμος), and his disciples having gone (πορεύομαι) to all the nations (ἔθνη) to have proclaimed (καταγγέλλω) his word, and further about [their] being about to be led (ἄγω) before governors (ἡγεμών) and kings for no other cause than his teaching (διδασκαλία), we are astonished at (τέθηπα) him and daily confirm (βεβαιόω) the faith (πίστις) in him. I do not know from what greater and clearer (ἐναργής) things Celsus wished him to make credible the things foretold (προλέγω); unless, as it appears, not understanding (ἐπίσταμαι) the doctrine (λόγος) [that] Jesus became man (ἄνθρωπος γενόμενος), he wished him to suffer nothing human and not to become for men a noble (γενναῖος) example concerning bearing (φέρω) what befalls (τὰ συμβαίνοντα). Even if these seem to Celsus most pitiable (οἴκτιστα) and most shameful (ἐπονειδιστότατα), since he knows pain (πόνος) as the greatest of evils and pleasure (ἡδονή) as the perfect good, which none of the philosophers introducing providence (πρόνοια) and agreeing that courage (ἀνδρεία) is virtue (ἀρετή), and endurance (καρτερία) and greatness of soul (μεγαλοψυχία), accepted (παραδέχομαι). Jesus therefore did not discredit (διαβάλλω) the faith in him through what he endured (ὑπομένω), but rather strengthened (κρατύνω) [it] among those wishing to accept (ἀποδέχομαι) courage, and among those taught by him that properly and truly living (ζῆν), the blessed (μακάριον), is not here but "in the" so-called according to his words "age to come" (μέλλων αἰών), and that living in the so-called present age (ἐνεστὼς αἰών) is a misfortune (συμφορά) or the first and greatest contest (ἀγών) of the soul.
pass_b_english: Further, since Celsus will have it that Jesus was not even blameless, let him prove it. Which of those who accepted his teaching recorded anything truly blameworthy in Jesus? Or, if he does not draw his charge of blame from them, let him show where he learned what led him to say that Jesus was not blameless.

Jesus, then, made what he promised credible by the good he did to those who gave heed to him. And as we see always being fulfilled what he said before it came to pass, that “the gospel” would “be preached” in the whole world (Matthew 26:13; compare Matthew 24:14; Mark 13:10), that his disciples would go to “all the nations” (Matthew 28:19) and proclaim his word, and further that they would be “led before governors and kings” (Matthew 10:18) for no other cause than his teaching, we stand in awe of him and daily confirm our faith in him. I do not know by what greater and clearer proofs Celsus wanted him to make credible what he had foretold; unless, as it seems, failing to understand the doctrine, he wanted Jesus, though he had become man, to suffer nothing human and not to become for men a noble example of how to bear what befalls them.

Even if these things seem to Celsus most pitiable and most shameful, since he holds pain to be the greatest of evils and pleasure the perfect good (a view that none of the philosophers who bring in providence, and who agree that courage is a virtue, and endurance and greatness of soul as well, has ever accepted), Jesus did not, for all that, discredit faith in him by what he endured. Rather, he strengthened it among those who wish to embrace courage, and among those who were taught by him that living in the proper and true sense, the blessed life, is not here but “in” what his words call “the age to come” (Matthew 12:32), while living in what is called the present age is a misfortune, or the first and greatest contest of the soul.

translator_notes: “Blameless” (ἀνεπίληπτον) and the request that Jesus “make credible” what he promised and foretold (πιστὰ ποιῆσαι) take up words of Celsus quoted just before; they are not set as quotations here because Origen gives them in indirect form. βούλεται here means “maintains, will have it”, not a wish. The “gospel ... in the whole world” wording (κηρυχθῆναι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ) matches Matthew 26:13 (Mark 14:9 has “into the whole world”; Matthew 24:14 has “in the whole inhabited earth”); the exact infinitive κηρυχθῆναι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον and “to all the nations” (εἰς πάντα τὰ ἔθνη) stand together in Mark 13:10, so it is added as “compare”. “Going ... to all the nations” (πορευθέντας ... πάντα τὰ ἔθνη) matches Matthew 28:19. “Before governors and kings” matches Matthew 10:18 (ἐπὶ ἡγεμόνας δὲ καὶ βασιλεῖς ἀχθήσεσθε; also Mark 13:9; Luke 21:12). μὴ ἐπιστάμενος τὸν λόγον τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἄνθρωπον γενόμενον ἐβούλετο μηδὲν ἀνθρώπινον παθεῖν is taken with τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἄνθρωπον γενόμενον as the subject of παθεῖν: “failing to understand the doctrine, he wanted Jesus, though he had become man, to suffer nothing human”; the earlier draft read “not understanding the teaching that Jesus became man”, which leaves παθεῖν without its subject. A reading “not understanding that the Word became man in Jesus” is grammatically possible but strains the word order. Koetschau’s stops after ἄρα and φαίνεται, and after ἐπονειδιστότατα, are read as commas: the κἂν clause is concessive and leads into οὐ διέβαλεν οὖν. “The age to come” (ἐν τῷ μέλλοντι [αἰῶνι]) is Jesus’ phrase in Matthew 12:32 (Mark 10:30 and Luke 18:30 say “the age that is coming”). The claim that Celsus holds pain the greatest evil and pleasure the perfect good is Origen’s polemic, consistent with his view of Celsus as an Epicurean; it is not a quotation of Celsus. τὸ μὲν κυρίως καὶ ἀληθῶς ζῆν τὸ μακάριον is rendered “living in the proper and true sense, the blessed life”, taking τὸ μακάριον in apposition.
